chapter: Army service and the 816th Pioneer Infantry Band
title: The band's players, Maurice Durand and the voyage to France
summary: White names his trumpet and other players, Durand's Livery Stable Blues feature, and the trip across England and France.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Oh. You guys, Maurice Durand was in that.
Yeah, yeah, he was right there. And Maurice Durand was a feature in that he could play the, the hook and car blues. And he, we had another, what that mule, piece in the other mule calls in it.
I don't remember, I remember some sort of race track numbers or what I say about that.
Well anyhow, he used to do the feature on that one.
Oh, there's Livery Stable. Livery Stable blues.

That was his, that was his big feature. And I would always call him out for that number. Yeah, he featured that and played it good too. And he had such strong, devilish lips. He didn't have the proper tone like Hatton had, Frank Hatton or Carl Travis or Robert Walker or Willie Triggs. See, I had ace trumpet players, good ones. They were very, very good. Willie Triggs was the outstanding trumpet player on the Georgia Misses before he came to the Army. And Robert D. Walker was a featured player in Handy's band. And Carl Travis was in Bill Berry's band in St. Louis. And they were good, very good. I didn't have any trouble with my trumpet players. And I had four fine melaphone players. And I had saxophones galore, plenty of them. I didn't have saxophones enough for them. Eddie T. Moore out of Tuskegee band was a bassoon and oboe player. They didn't give us any bassoon. So he played baritone sax. And he did justice to it always. The band was well, well qualified. And while in France, why, I told you that we had to play for this 33rd Division passing in review, they had no band capable of passing them in review and observing all the signals of an officer. Well, I had a fellow named George Wells. He'd been in the 10th Cavalry. He's tall, very handsome youngster. And he knew all the signals for a band, for a observance of an officer in review passing. And he carried them out to the left. While I only stood to the left of my band, you know. And we stayed in this review passing for, oh, from 9 o'clock in the morning until after 4 in the afternoon. Then we hiked on down to Southampton. And all of this hiking, we played limited long drives in England also, in cities as we passed through them. And we crossed the channel at midnight there for La Havre, France. We got over in La Havre while we were underground trains, straight on up through the middle of Paris. And when we got right near this big city of Lille, which was a railroad center in France, then we came up, surfaced up. It was well guarded around there. They were all watching for the Germans to attack them any time. And right out from Lille, we had to go underground again and dugouts and so forth. So we just went on a crawling train on what they call now the 40 and 8. That boxcar that holds 12 hogs. No. Yeah, 12 hogs, 8 horses, or 24 men. Chavez hombres, you see. I don't, I've forgotten what they call a horse, but anyhow, it's a swine name in French. I forgot my French. I could remember it easily by referring to some of the old records.
Yeah. Cochon. Cochon. Yeah. Yeah. 8 horses, 12 cochons. 12 hogs. Oh yeah, 24 hombres.
